qs.q: An infant is born with a flat, light pink lesion on the forehead that gradually grows, thickens the overlying skin during childhood, and persists over time. Further evaluation reveals it is in the trigeminal nerve distribution. What diagnosis should be suspected?
qs.e: A port wine stain is a type of nevus flammeus that tends to grow during childhood, thicken the skin, and persist. When located in the trigeminal nerve distribution, it is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome, caused by a somatic GNAQ missense mutation.

qs.q: A newborn infant presents with a flat, pink-to-purple macular patch on the face located within the distribution of the ophthalmic and maxillary branches of the trigeminal nerve. What is the most critical associated neurological condition to investigate?
o: Ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas affecting the brain
Disseminated intravascular coagulation from visceral cancer
Chronic venous insufficiency with painful stasis ulcers
qs.e: A port wine stain in the trigeminal distribution strongly suggests Sturge-Weber syndrome, which is characterized by ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas and neurological symptoms. The other options are unrelated pathologies involving different vascular or neoplastic mechanisms.

qs.q: A port wine stain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve is found in a child with seizures, intellectual disability, and skull "tram-track" calcifications. What underlying mutation causes this syndrome?
o: Germline VHL mutation causing haemangioblastomas and arteriovenous malformations
NF1 mutation causing multiple neurofibromas and characteristic café-au-lait macules
Somatic GNAQ missense mutation in the Gα subunit causing constitutive intracellular signalling
TSC1/TSC2 mutation causing tuberous sclerosis complex with characteristic cortical tubers
qs.e: Sturge-Weber syndrome (port wine stain + leptomeningeal angiomas + seizures + intellectual disability) is caused by a somatic GNAQ missense mutation occurring early in development — not inherited.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is the main sensory and motor nerve of the face, branching into ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular divisions. It supplies sensation, mastication and facial expression. Understanding its anatomy guides diagnosis of facial pain, nerve injury and cranial infections.

sections.p: The trigeminal nerve is the largest cranial nerve, carrying both sensory and motor fibers. It emerges from the pons, enters the skull through the foramen ovale, and divides into three branches that supply the face and oral cavity.

It originates from the pontine tegmentum, travels through the middle cranial fossa, and exits the skull via the foramen ovale (mandibular) and foramen rotundum (maxillary). The ophthalmic branch exits through the superior orbital fissure.
Adjacent to the internal carotid artery, middle meningeal artery, and the cavernous sinus. The mandibular branch passes through the infratemporal fossa, close to the mandibular condyle.
b: Shares space with middle meningeal artery

sections.p: Supplied by branches of the middle meningeal artery and the ophthalmic artery.
Sensory fibers travel with the ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular divisions; motor fibers are confined to the mandibular division.
Provides facial sensation, controls mastication muscles, and contributes to facial expression.
Injury can cause facial numbness, loss of chewing, or trigeminal neuralgia. Infections like herpes zoster ophthalmicus involve V1 and risk keratitis.

t.b: Detects compressive lesions (e.g., tumor) causing neuralgia; abnormal if enhancing mass seen

sections.p: Remember that V3 carries motor fibers; loss of jaw closure suggests mandibular branch damage. V1 lesions present with ocular complications.

whenToSeekHelp: Trigeminal neuralgia with sudden severe pain, loss of facial sensation, or ocular involvement such as keratitis or vision loss

faq.a: Compression by a blood vessel, tumor, or demyelination (multiple sclerosis).

faq.q: How is herpes zoster ophthalmicus treated?
faq.a: Antiviral therapy within 72 hours and topical steroids for ocular inflammation.

faq.q: Can the trigeminal nerve be repaired?
faq.a: Surgical decompression or nerve grafting may relieve symptoms but full recovery is uncommon.
